1) Symptomatic expanding infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (impending rupture/contained leak) — 5.3 cm AAA with thrombus + month of abdominal/back pain makes this the most likely cause.  
2) Ruptured AAA with retroperitoneal hematoma (contained or ongoing bleed) — similar presentation; less likely if CTA showed no active extravasation, but remains high-risk.  
3) Aortic mural thrombus → embolic or branch occlusion causing mesenteric ischemia — thrombus present on CTA; can cause persistent abdominal pain, especially in older patients.  
4) Acute pancreatitis — classically causes epigastric pain radiating to the back and is a common mimic; needs enzyme testing to confirm/exclude.  
5) Peptic ulcer disease with posterior penetration (duodenal/gastric) or other upper GI pathology — can produce epigastric pain radiating to the back and should be considered.

Immediate recommended next steps (urgent): assess hemodynamics and abdominal exam (pulsatile mass, tenderness), obtain bedside abdominal aortic ultrasound if not already seen on CTA images, serial vitals, and urgent vascular surgery consultation. Key tests to order to refine diagnosis: serum hemoglobin/hematocrit, type & crossmatch, serum lactate, serum lipase, basic metabolic panel, and repeat/contrast CT review for extravasation.
